prompt: `Desk.java` called `poll` a fourth time on a queue that had held three people. What happened?

choices.text: It threw `NoSuchElementException` and the program ended
choices.why: That is `remove()` on an empty queue; `poll` answers instead of throwing.

choices.text: It answered `null`
choices.why: Right: the program printed `poll    null` and carried on.

choices.text: It answered `Ana` again, starting over from the head
choices.why: A queue does not cycle; what was polled is gone.

prompt: Match each throwing method of `Queue` to its special-value twin.
hint: The table at the top of the section.

prompt: The two-seat `ArrayBlockingQueue` already held two people. `offer("Carla")` answered `false`. Why did `add("Carla")` then end the program?

choices.text: Calling `offer` first had left the queue in a broken state
choices.why: The queue was simply full; nothing was broken, and `offer` changed nothing.

choices.text: `add` throws `IllegalStateException` when the queue is full
choices.why: Right: `Queue full`, from line 24, and nothing caught it.

choices.text: `add` is not allowed on a queue from `java.util.concurrent`
choices.why: It is allowed; it is the throwing form of `offer`, and it threw because the queue was full.

choices.text: Carla was already in the queue, and a queue refuses duplicates
choices.why: Queues accept duplicates; Carla was never in it, because `offer` refused her.

prompt: Why can a queue whose `poll` answers `null` for "empty" not usefully hold `null` elements?

choices.text: Because `null` takes no memory, so it cannot be stored
choices.why: A `null` reference occupies a slot like any other; the problem is what it would mean.

choices.text: Because the compiler forbids `Queue<String>` from holding `null`
choices.why: Generics say nothing about `null`; `ArrayDeque` refuses it at run time.

choices.text: A `null` from `poll` could no longer tell an empty queue from a `null` element
choices.why: Right: the special value only works if it is never a real element.

prompt: `Holds.java` printed its `PriorityQueue` and Eva, with 3 days, came last. What is the printed order?

choices.text: The order of the heap's array, which only guarantees the smallest at the front
choices.why: Right: `toString` walks the array as it lies; only `poll` gives the priority order.

choices.text: Insertion order, as in a `LinkedHashSet`
choices.why: Bruno went in first and was printed fourth.

choices.text: Sorted order, with a bug in `toString`
choices.why: No bug: a heap is not sorted, and `toString` promises nothing about priority.

choices.text: Alphabetical order of the members' names
choices.why: Ana would have come first; Carla did.

prompt: Put the holds in the order `poll` handed them out.
A print queue must never be empty when a printer asks for work; if it is, something upstream has failed. Which call should the printer use to take the next job?
hint: Is an empty queue normal here, or a mistake?

choices.text: `poll()`, and carry on quietly if it answers `null`
choices.why: An empty queue here is a failure upstream, and carrying on quietly hides it.

choices.text: `remove()`, which throws when the queue is empty
choices.why: Right: the situation is a mistake, so the throwing form makes it visible where it happens.

choices.text: `peek()`, which does not change the queue
choices.why: `peek` only looks; the printer still has to take the job out.

choices.text: `pop()`, because a print queue is a stack
choices.why: Jobs print in the order they arrived; that is a queue, and `pop` takes the newest.

prompt: Three actions were pushed onto the `ArrayDeque`: `lend Dune`, `lend Emma`, `return Dune`. What did the first `pop` give?

choices.text: `lend Dune`, the first action
choices.why: That is what a queue would give; a stack gives the newest.

choices.text: `lend Emma`, the one in the middle
choices.why: `peek` showed `lend Emma` after the pop, as the new top.

choices.text: `return Dune`
choices.why: Right: the last action pushed is the first undone.

prompt: On a `Deque`, `push(e)` is another name for `___(e)`, and `pop()` for `removeFirst()`.
`old.add(0, "slipped in at the bottom")` compiled on a `Stack<String>`. Why?

choices.text: `Stack` adds `add(int, E)` so that stacks can be built from the bottom
choices.why: `Stack` declares five methods of its own, and that is not one of them.

choices.text: `Stack` extends `Vector`, a list, and inherits its list methods
choices.why: Right: every list method is a way into the middle of the stack, and the compiler allows each one.

choices.text: Java does not check method calls on legacy classes
choices.why: The compiler checks every call; this one exists, inherited.

prompt: Which of these are reasons the section gives for using `ArrayDeque` rather than `Stack`? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two are about inheritance, one is about cost.

choices.text: `Stack` inherits list methods that reach into the middle
choices.why: Yes: `add(0, …)` and `get(0)` broke the stack in the program.

choices.text: `Stack`'s methods are synchronized, and pay for locking on every call
choices.why: Yes: `Vector`'s methods lock whether or not two threads ever share it.

choices.text: `Stack` was removed in Java 25
choices.why: It is still there, kept for compatibility with old code.

choices.text: The JDK's own documentation recommends `Deque` for stacks
choices.why: Yes: `Stack`'s documentation points at `Deque` itself.

choices.text: `ArrayDeque` keeps its elements sorted
choices.why: It keeps them in the order the two ends were used; sorting is `PriorityQueue`'s business, or `TreeSet`'s.

prompt: The deque printed `[return Dune, lend Emma, lend Dune]` and the `Stack` `[lend Dune, lend Emma, return Dune]`, for the same three pushes. Why opposite orders?
hint: Where does each one keep its top?

choices.text: The deque prints from its head, the top; the `Stack` prints as a `Vector`, from index 0
choices.why: Right: same stack, two ways of laying it out, and only the deque's matches the order of undoing.

choices.text: The `Stack` reversed them because `pop` had been called once
choices.why: Both were printed before any `pop`; the order comes from where each keeps its top.

choices.text: `push` on a `Stack` adds at the head and on a deque at the tail
choices.why: It is the other way round in storage, and either way both hand back the newest first.

prompt: Which class does the section recommend behind a `Queue<E>` that is first come, first served?
hint: The same class as for a stack.

choices.text: `LinkedList`
choices.why: It implements `Queue`, and it lost every round of the measurement.

choices.text: `PriorityQueue`
choices.why: That one serves the smallest first, not the first to arrive.

choices.text: `ArrayDeque`
choices.why: Right: a reused array with its ends wrapping round, and no node per element.

choices.text: `Stack`
choices.why: A stack serves the last to arrive.

prompt: Why did the `LinkedList` lose to the `ArrayDeque` at a queue's job, in both rounds?
hint: What does each `offer` cost the linked list?

choices.text: Its `poll` has to walk to the end of the list
choices.why: It keeps a link to both ends, so `poll` is one step; the cost is elsewhere.

choices.text: Every `offer` allocates a node, and the garbage collector clears millions
choices.why: Right: the deque writes into a reused array instead.

choices.text: The JIT compiler cannot compile `LinkedList` methods
choices.why: The JIT compiles them like any others; the work they do is what costs.

prompt: In the measurement the `ArrayDeque` was faster in its second round than in its first, and the `LinkedList` was not. What explains the `ArrayDeque`'s second round?

choices.text: Its array was already full from the first round
choices.why: Each round created a new `ArrayDeque`; nothing carried over but the compiled code.

choices.text: By then the JIT had compiled the hot loop and methods
choices.why: Right: the first round ran partly interpreted.

choices.text: The second round pushed fewer numbers through the queue
choices.why: Both rounds pushed the same five million.

prompt: A browser's back button returns to the most recently visited page. Which declaration fits the history?

choices.text: `Deque<String> history = new ArrayDeque<>();`
choices.why: Right: a stack, used through `push` and `pop`.

choices.text: `Queue<String> history = new ArrayDeque<>();`
choices.why: Through `Queue`, `poll` gives the oldest page, not the newest.

choices.text: `Stack<String> history = new Stack<>();`
choices.why: It works, and it is the class section 03 told you to leave behind.

choices.text: `Queue<String> history = new PriorityQueue<>();`
choices.why: A priority queue would hand back pages in alphabetical order.

prompt: `QueueCost` kept the queue at most how many elements long?
hint: Look at the `if` inside the loop.

prompt: An emergency room sees patients by severity, and among equal severities by arrival. Which is closest to right?
hint: Which queue serves by an order you choose?

choices.text: An `ArrayDeque`, with the severe patients added at the front with `offerFirst`
choices.why: Two severe patients would then be seen newest first, the reverse of arrival.

choices.text: A `PriorityQueue` whose comparator states both rules, the second breaking ties
choices.why: Right: the comparator states the whole rule, and `poll` follows it.

choices.text: A `TreeSet`, since it keeps patients sorted
choices.why: A set drops two patients that compare equal, which a hospital cannot do.

prompt: A `for-each` over a `PriorityQueue` prints its elements. In what order do they come?
hint: It is the same walk `toString` does.

choices.text: Smallest first, as `poll` would give them
choices.why: Only repeated `poll` gives that order; iteration does not.

choices.text: In the heap array's order
choices.why: Right: the smallest first, and the rest in no promised order.

choices.text: In the order they were offered
choices.why: Bruno was offered first and printed fourth in `Holds.java`.

prompt: Which class from this lesson accepts `null` as an element?

choices.text: `ArrayDeque`
choices.why: It refuses `null` with a `NullPointerException`.

choices.text: `PriorityQueue`
choices.why: It cannot compare `null` and refuses it.

choices.text: `LinkedList`
choices.why: Right: and section 02 said why a queue should not hold one anyway.

choices.text: `ArrayBlockingQueue`
choices.why: The concurrent queues refuse `null` too.
